title: Punjab in the early 1980s
hookLine: political demands, rising violence and armed militants inside the Harmandir complex, led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, a figure Sikhs see very differently, brought crisis

lines: AN ARGUMENT THAT STARTS WITH SOMETHING REAL.
cards: Some arguments start with something real: money, fairness, who gets a say. Nobody listens. Voices rise.
A door slams. Then something happens that can't be taken back, and years later everyone involved tells the story differently, each holding a true piece of it.
Punjab at the start of the 1980s was something like that, but with a whole state, a national government and many lives at stake.

teach.h: THE DEMANDS: POWER, WATER, A CAPITAL.
teach.b: It began with politics. In 1973 the Akali Dal, the main Sikh party, passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, asking for more power for the states and for Chandigarh to be Punjab's.
By the early 1980s, a fair share of Punjab's river waters was among the demands too. Governments in Delhi saw some of it as a threat to the nation. Talks went nowhere.
In 1982 the Akalis began a new morcha, and tens of thousands of Sikhs courted arrest. Into this stepped Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, the head of a traditional Sikh school, the Damdami Taksal.
A powerful preacher, he called Sikhs back to amrit, to their practice, away from drink and drugs, and spoke fiercely about injustice to Sikhs.
Meanwhile, violence grew in Punjab: killings of Hindus, of Sikhs who disagreed, of police, and hard police action in return.
From 1982 Bhindranwale lived inside the Harmandir Sahib complex, and in December 1983 he and armed followers moved into the Akal Takht, which was fortified in the months that followed.
Here is where to hold the whole story.

Sikhs see Bhindranwale very differently. Some honor him as a saint and a martyr who stood up for a community they felt was treated unjustly. Other Sikhs believe his path, and weapons in the holiest place, led to disaster.
The Indian government called him a terrorist. People in Punjab of every faith lived in fear in those years. This lesson doesn't settle who was right.
It asks you to hold the demands, the grievances, the violence and the fear all at once, because they were all there.

how: Sikhs hold a range of views on the early 1980s and on Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale; in gurdwaras and families these years are usually discussed with care, and often with strong feeling.

o: a party's written list of demands
a peaceful campaign of mass protest
an armed uprising against the state

games.q: the pieces of the crisis — tap the pairs.

s: the crisis began with political demands
power for the states and Chandigarh were in the 1973 resolution; river waters joined the demands later.
all Sikhs see Bhindranwale the same way
some honor him as a saint and martyr; other Sikhs believe his path led to disaster.
only one community lived in fear in those years
people in Punjab of every faith lived in fear.

games.q: a friend asks you to sum up Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale in one word. what does this lesson suggest?
o: no one word: Sikhs see him very differently.
games.why: some Sikhs honor him as a saint and martyr, others believe his path led to disaster, and the government called him a terrorist. the lesson holds the whole story.

practice: Think of a conflict you know, in your family, your town or the news, where people you respect disagree, and picture one person from each side telling you what they're afraid of.
Don't decide who wins; just notice that fear and hurt live on both sides of most arguments. If you feel yourself taking a side, gently widen the frame again.

wordCard.voice: Morcha. A peaceful campaign of protest — in the early 1980s, amid political demands, rising violence, and armed militants in the Harmandir complex, around a leader Sikhs see very differently.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: morcha, a campaign or front; the Akalis' way of peaceful mass protest.

carryVoice: Your line: hold the whole story. This one doesn't fit in a single word. Day three hundred seven.
